summary:
Huancavelica stands under Peru's national framework. The region has no recorded trans-specific statute, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident of its own, so what a trans visitor to Huancavelica faces is the national position: no criminalisation of trans identity, statutory restriction of access to public facilities, no hate-crime protection for LGBT people, and rising recorded violence.

Peru's Congress legislated directly against trans people's use of public restrooms. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved, exempting it from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject only to narrow listed exceptions. The measure reached the floor through the Women and Family Commission, which on 20 February 2025 unanimously approved a merged draft opinion (dictamen) of bills 6506 and 8457 introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante; that draft barred trans people from restrooms not corresponding to their birth sex, allowed exceptions for custody, required medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and banned 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The legal analysis of IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that the restriction violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. LGTBIQ activist and trans journalist Gianna Camacho warned that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

Recorded violence against trans people is rising and under-counted. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023. Trans women were more than half the homicide victims, at 30, followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of which 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty such as multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denunciations filed in 2020 alone.

One case illustrates the pattern and its slow remedy. In February 2023 a gang abducted Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, in central Lima and killed her in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
Hate-crime protection for LGBT people was stripped from Peru's Penal Code in 2017, when Congress voted to remove the provisions after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Regional standards point the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The Azul Rojas Marín case reached that Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and, per BBC News Mundo, became the Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Enforcement of the bathroom restriction reaches private life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. Congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons on the floor of Congress, recorded by IDEHPUCP.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained by vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content that enables censorship of identity, artistic and educational material; the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
The April 2025 restriction and the signage ban bind residents of Huancavelica as much as visitors: regional authorities, businesses and public institutions in the region apply the national rule on 'biological sex' for restroom access, with no local ordinance softening or widening it on record.

Residents also live with the absence of hate-crime coverage. The 2017 repeal means killings and assaults motivated by anti-LGBT animus are not charged as hate crimes under the Penal Code, which shapes how the 54 homicides and 170 rights-violation cases recorded for 2020-2023 were processed.

Healthcare settings changed on paper in June 2024, when health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance. Whether facilities in Huancavelica apply the revised terminology is not addressed by the sources.

Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 hate-crime reporting, has stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry, so residents' lived exposure to violence is higher than official counts suggest.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Huancavelica-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding appears in the sources: the region's assessment rests entirely on national data, and whether security staff, gyms, clinics or municipal facilities in Huancavelica have applied the bathroom rule, and how, is unresolved.

The sources do not resolve whether the exception list in the February 2025 committee draft (custody, medical attention, accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities) was carried verbatim into the article 5 text approved by the Plenary on 2 April 2025, nor whether the draft's ban on 'ambiguous' signage matches the enacted wording on inclusive signage.

Document and gender-marker change rules, visa and entry screening that could out a traveller, partner recognition, and access to trans-related healthcare in Huancavelica are not sourced in this inventory and remain unaddressed.

The 170 rights-violation cases and 54 homicides are national totals with no regional breakdown, so their distribution across Huancavelica is unknown; the sub-registry caveat raised by Gianna Camacho applies to them.
